output:
*Interview with Rosa Häfeli, maid and cook, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Sit down, Mademoiselle Häfeli. You are not in any trouble. I only want you to tell me about the kitchen, in your own words.

ROSA: Ja, Herr Inspektor. I am not used to sitting in this room. I am always in the kitchen.

MATTHEY: Then tell me about the kitchen.

ROSA: The champagne glasses were on the tray by the stove, all polished. The pastries were done. Madame said the glasses must shine, so they shone. I did not sit down once, Herrgott, not once.

MATTHEY: Is there a clock in the kitchen?

ROSA: Ja, the American alarm clock on the shelf over the table. It is a cheap thing, but I keep it fast on purpose. When the temple struck ten, my kitchen clock showed a quarter past ten. Nothing in this house should be late, Herr Inspektor. So I set the clock early, and then I am never caught out.

MATTHEY: Did anyone come down to the kitchen?

ROSA: Fräulein Lina came down into the kitchen at twenty-three minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock. She did not say why. She was very white and sat by the stove, and she stayed with me until after the temple struck eleven. She is a quiet girl. Her hands were shaking, I saw it, but she would not talk.

MATTHEY: What did you hear while you were in the kitchen?

ROSA: We heard Madame's piano begin at twelve minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock. It was the Chopin, the slow one. Madame plays it very well. I know that piece. It stopped at one minute past eleven by my kitchen clock.

MATTHEY: Did you hear the hall clock?

ROSA: Ja. I heard the hall clock strike eleven when my kitchen clock showed three minutes past eleven. That old Morbier, it strikes by its own face. You can hear it all through the house.

MATTHEY: Thank you. Now tell me about going up to the atelier.

ROSA: The glasses were ready, and Madame wanted him down.

MATTHEY: Do you know what time it was when you went up?

ROSA: No, Herr Inspektor. I was not looking at any clock. I was looking for the master.

MATTHEY: Tell me what you saw.

ROSA: He was on the floor by his bench, under the long windows. The regulator on the wall had stopped. The brass mallet from his bench was lying there on the boards. His repeater was in his hand. I thought he had fallen. I thought he was ill, that he had only fainted.

MATTHEY: Did you touch him?

ROSA: I touched his hand. It was cold. I called out, I think. I do not remember what I said. Then the doctor was called, and the police, and now I am in this room.

MATTHEY: Are you afraid of me, Mademoiselle Häfeli?

ROSA: Ja. I am only the maid. I have never been near the police in my life, and I know what happens to people like me when there is a dead man in the house. I have done nothing. I have a clean kitchen and I have always kept it clean.

MATTHEY: I understand. Tell me about Madame.

ROSA: Madame has been good to me. She is hard, but she is fair, and she does not shout. I will not say anything about her that is not true. And I will not say anything that is not so about anyone else either, not Fräulein Lina, not Monsieur Félix, not anybody.

MATTHEY: That is all I ask. Thank you, Mademoiselle Häfeli. You may go back to your kitchen for now.

ROSA: Danke, Herr Inspektor. Madame will want the glasses taken up.
